author: blu
body: THE ARITHMETIC IS BORROWED, THE CURVE IS NOT. Every big-number operation here runs through `Foreword chapter CryptoBig`: base 2^16 limbs, Montgomery reduction, no division. That chapter was written for RSA and needs nothing added for this, which is the reason it is used rather than a second bignum being written beside it. What this chapter adds is the field layer CryptoBig has no opinion about (addition, subtraction and inversion modulo a prime) and the group layer above it.

author: blu
body: p - 2 is the exponent that inverts a field element by Fermat's little theorem. Inversion is needed twice per verification and a binary extended Euclid would be faster, but this way the only reduction primitive in the chapter is Montgomery's, and a second one is a second thing that can be subtly wrong.

author: blu
body: A field is its modulus in limbs together with the three values Montgomery multiplication needs. They are computed once per verification and threaded, rather than recomputed per operation: `cb-r-squared` doubles thirty-two times per limb, so recomputing it inside the point loop would cost more than the point loop.

author: blu
body: The curve's own constants ride on the field rather than being read from the top of the chapter. The field is already threaded through every function that needs them, so this adds no parameter anywhere, and it is what makes one copy of the arithmetic serve both curves. `ef-b`, `ef-gx` and `ef-gy` are empty for a field built over the group order, which never sees the curve equation.

author: blu
body: Multiplication is Montgomery's, so both operands and the result are in Montgomery form and the form is never mixed. Addition and subtraction need no conversion at all: x maps to xR, and that map is linear, so a sum of Montgomery forms is the Montgomery form of the sum.

author: blu
body: A sum that overflowed the top limb is above the modulus however the low limbs compare, so the carry is tested before the comparison rather than instead of it.

author: blu
body: Subtraction that goes negative wraps by adding the modulus back. The borrow out of the top limb is exactly the test for that, and it is returned rather than clamped for the same reason CryptoBig's subtraction carries its borrow explicitly.

author: blu
body: Inversion by Fermat: a^(p-2) is a^-1 for every non-zero a modulo a prime. `cb-mod-exp-bytes` works on plain byte strings rather than Montgomery limbs, so the value leaves Montgomery form on the way in and returns to it on the way out. That is two conversions for one inversion, and it happens once per verification, not once per point.

author: blu
body: Addition of two Jacobian points. The intermediates are gathered into a record rather than threaded as parameters because the formula needs six of them alive at once and a nine-parameter helper is harder to read than the arithmetic it carries. The record costs one allocation against the eleven multiplications around it.

author: blu
body: Double and add, most significant bit first, starting at the scalar's highest set bit. Starting above it would square in leading zeros, which is harmless and slow; a scalar of zero has no set bit and answers infinity, which is what `cb-top-bit` returning minus one arranges.

author: blu
body: A public key is checked before it is used. Two independent things are required: each coordinate must be a field element, and the point must satisfy the curve equation.

author: blu
body: Multiplication modulo n of two plain values. Montgomery multiplication answers a*b*R^-1, so multiplying that by R^2 and reducing once more gives a*b with both operands and the result outside Montgomery form. Two reductions to avoid carrying a form through six lines is the right trade at this call count.

author: blu
body: s inverse modulo n, then u1 = z/s and u2 = r/s, both reduced to plain byte strings because the scalar multiplication reads bits off bytes.
